data.title: Middle East Eye: UN says IMO confirms 25 seafarer deaths since Iran war began
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
UN says IMO confirms 25 seafarer deaths since Iran war began
As many as 25 seafarers have been killed in 134 confirmed maritime incidents across the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the US and Israeli started war on Iran in February, according to Khalid Khiari, UN Assistant Secretary-General Khaled for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific.
Briefing the UN Security Council on Friday, Khiari cited figures from the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) covering incidents recorded up to November 11.
He said October saw the highest monthly number of incidents involving commercial shipping since February, warning that continued disruption was driving up energy, transport and insurance costs and threatening global food security.
“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” Khiari said, calling for an immediate end to attacks on civilian vessels and the restoration of safe maritime navigation.
Bahrain’s representative told the meeting that about 1,600 vessels had been affected by disruptions in the waterway, leaving more than 23,000 seafarers stranded aboard their ships.
Bhargavi Suresh and her two sons sit in front of the photograph of her dead husband, Patnala Suresh, at their home in Visakhapatnam, India, on 23 June 2026 (Aatif Ammad/MEE)

data.title: Middle East Eye: Mossad chief in Washington for talks on Iran, report says
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Mossad chief in Washington for talks on Iran, report says
Roman Gofman, chief of Israeli spy agency Mossad and one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, was in Washington on Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran, Axios reported, citing three sources with knowledge of the matter.
The visit comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Axios said Gofman was to meet CIA Director John Ratcliffe and later expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff.
Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment, Axios said.
Meanwhile Israel's Channel 12 news reported that Gofman’s trip was not disclosed to Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot in his Thursday security briefing with Netanyahu.
Trump, who suffered a defeat in the midterm elections, has resisted the pressure to resume strikes on Iran. Also, on Friday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that further military action against Iran was unnecessary because the "economic pain" inflicted by the US sanctions on Tehran "was so great".

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'What would be left of international legal order': Araghchi on US strikes
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
'What would be left of international legal order': Araghchi on US strikes
"If states were free to attack one another based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has asked in an opinion piece for Japan's Kyodo News.
"This question," Araghchi wrote, "goes well beyond the political dispute between Iran and the United States."
"It concerns one of the fundamental principles on which the international order established after the Second World War rests: the use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," the article read.
He said the US-Israeli strikes constituted a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty.
"Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun," he wrote.
He said the US had neither obtained UN Security Council authorisation nor established grounds for invoking self-defence under Article 51, which permits force in response to an armed attack.
The attacks on schools, sports stadiums, civilian infrastructure, and Iranian nuclear facilities subject to International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards raise further questions under international law, and they must be examined under international humanitarian law.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UKMTO says seven Hormuz tanker attacks recorded in a week
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
UKMTO says seven Hormuz tanker attacks recorded in a week
At least seven tankers were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the week to 11 November, UKMTO said, with one strike leaving multiple crew injured in the Arabian Gulf.
The latest, on 11 November, hit a tanker’s engine room 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras al-Khaimah, and the crew was evacuated, UKMTO said in its weekly overview.
Of eight incidents reported, three vessels continued their voyage, three needed assistance and two had unknown outcomes. None was reported sunk.
On 7 November, US Central Command said it disabled the HUDA in the Gulf of Oman after its crew ignored warnings and tried to breach the US naval blockade.
UKMTO said the traffic through the waterway was about 65 percent below pre-war levels, with combined 139 outbound and 169 inbound transits, against 170 and 155 the previous week. It rated threat level in the strait is as severe.
In the Red Sea, no attacks have been reported since 24 August, but Bab al-Mandab transits remain about 24 percent below levels before the Houthis’ 22 July blockade announcement.
UKMTO has logged 163 conflict-related incidents since 28 February.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran says three tankers hit by mines in Hormuz catch fire
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Iran says three tankers hit by mines in Hormuz catch fire
Iran's navy and Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorised route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Guards' navy said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker "navigating through the unsafe and prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking and identification systems switched off, caught fire and was forced to stop after striking a naval mine".
The statements did not provide the names or origins of the vessels but the Guards said one of those hit in south Hormuz was a supertanker.
The Guards released footage on Friday of a large plume of smoke rising from a vessel it said was carrying liquefied gas and hit a mine in the south of the strait.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rubio targets ICC: 'Won't submit to sterile vision of radical judges'
data.author: Hilal Saki
data.summary:
Rubio targets ICC: 'Won't submit to sterile vision of radical judges'
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has targeted the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a speech to a conservative legal group on Friday, arguing for a muscular foreign policy and against international law restraining US actions.
During his speech to the Federalist Society in Washington, his first prepared remarks since Republicans were routed in the midterm elections on 3 November, Rubio said the goal of the US-Israeli war against Iran was to prevent Tehran from ever developing a nuclear weapon, which he said was particularly urgent because the Islamic Republic's "radical Shia clerics" had an "expansionist mentality."
He contrasted this with the government of North Korea's Kim Jong Un, whom Trump has met three times. "I'm not excusing the terrible things that have happened there," Rubio said of North Korea. "I'm just saying he (Kim) is not expansionist. He's not trying to invade Japan or, you know, China or whatever."
Rubio dismissed criticisms that the Trump administration has broken international law by such actions as seizing Venezuelan then-President Nicolas Maduro and striking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific that it says were carrying drugs.
The US, Rubio said, would not “submit to the sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats,” repeating his assertion that the court would try to prosecute US officials or service members that he used to justify sanctions against the ICC announced last month.
“Americans have never agreed to submit to the ICC's authority, but that court and its allies in the global bureaucracy have appointed themselves judge and jury and executioner of the international order,” Rubio said.
The Trump ​administration has long been hostile to the Netherlands-based court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.

Amnesty International has urged the newly formed government in Pakistan-controlled Kashmir to release hundreds of activists arbitrarily detained under anti-terrorism laws for protesting against the rising cost of living.
In a letter to the newly elected Prime Minister Syed Iftikhar Ali Gilani, the rights group demanded that Gilani’s new administration improve the human rights situation by repealing the ban on the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).
“In [the] wake of swift and systematic steps taken by authorities since June in the region to repress civic freedoms, we call upon your government and all relevant authorities to ensure that the human rights of all those inside the region are upheld,” wrote Isabelle Lassee, deputy regional director at Amnesty’s South Asia Regional Office.
“The arbitrary banning of Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots people’s movement, by proscribing it under the first schedule of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Anti-Terrorism Act, 2014 violates the right to association, freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
Founded in 2023, JAAC is a coalition of traders, lawyers, students, civil society activists and local political figures who have campaigned against the high electricity bills, rising flour prices, heavy taxation and poor public services affecting Kashmiris in Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

data.author: MEE staff

US air travel thrown into chaos as nationwide flights grounded over 'radar instability'
Submitted by
MEE staff
on

The FAA lifted the ground stop after more than four hours, but officials warned that flight disruptions would continue as airlines worked to restore operations
A passenger walks past a plane at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport during a nationwide ground stop following a communications outage in Washington, DC, on 13 November 2026 (Brendan Smialowski/AFP)
Off
Chaos was reported at airports across the United States on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights following problems with radar and communications systems.
Passengers were stranded as hundreds of flights were diverted and thousands cancelled.
Officials said instability in radar systems made it unsafe to continue normal operations.
The FAA said in a statement that communications problems had affected multiple air traffic control centres and that technicians were investigating.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the disruption began at 3.36pm EST (8.36pm GMT), when radar and communications systems at facilities across the country became unstable.
“We started to have inconsistency in the data from the radars and our communication with airplanes,” Duffy said at a White House briefing.
He said more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the ground stop was imposed. Those planes were allowed to continue to their destinations and land safely.
The FAA lifted the restriction at 8.15pm, but Duffy warned that restoring normal operations would take time.
“It's going to be slow,” he said, urging passengers to check with their airlines as carriers worked to reposition aircraft and crews.
The disruption came a day after a global Microsoft outage affected services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, disrupting government operations and businesses worldwide.

Diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries condemn Israeli strike on Nasser hospital
Top diplomats from 18 Muslim-majority countries strongly condemned an Israeli strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.
Countries that condemned the strike include Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Egypt, Turkey, and Pakistan.
The attack left at least six people dead, including a child and a surgeon, prompting accusations from ministers that Israel is violating international humanitarian law.
In the joint declaration, the foreign ministers condemned ongoing assaults against Palestinians, warning that violence threatens to collapse the ceasefire in Gaza.
The countries accused Israel of blockading critical humanitarian assistance- specifically medical shipments and winter supplies-which they warned leaves infants and children exposed to failing water, sanitation, and healthcare systems as winter sets in.
Pressing for immediate compliance, the coalition called on Israel to strictly enforce the truce, facilitate unhindered aid deliveries, and fully honour its obligations under the ceasefire framework.

Huang’s departure, announced on 12 November, took effect immediately. Nvidia’s board appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while it searches for a permanent successor.
The company said it would consider both internal and external candidates.
Israeli media have named Michael Kagan, Nvidia’s chief technology officer; Eyal Waldman, co-founder and former chief executive of Israeli networking company Mellanox; and Johny Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, as possible contenders.
Kagan co-founded Mellanox in 1999 and joined Nvidia after it acquired the company in 2020 for about $6.9bn.
He has since served as Nvidia’s chief technology officer, focusing on technologies that allow thousands of processors to communicate within large data centres.
Waldman also co-founded Mellanox and served as its chief executive before the acquisition. Unlike Kagan, he is no longer part of Nvidia’s management.
Ynet has also reported that he is in the succession discussions.
Srouji, Apple’s chief hardware officer, is one of the key figures behind the company’s in-house chip development.
He joined Apple in 2008 and led the development of processors used in its products, including those underpinning its transition from Intel processors to Apple Silicon.

Removals include the commander of a destroyer deployed to support operations against Iran and three senior members of an attack submarine’s command team.
US Marines and sailors prepare F-35B fighter jets for flight operations aboard the USS Essex in the US Fifth Fleet’s area of operations on 27 September 2018 (AFP)
Off
The US Navy has fired several top officers without its customary public announcements, drawing criticism from lawmakers amid heightened security concerns at American military installations and tensions with Iran.
Those removed include the leadership team of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota. Its commander, second-in-command and senior enlisted sailor were relieved of their duties in October after the submarine reportedly struck something on the seabed.
The Navy also sacked Commander Caitlin Cunningham from her position leading the USS Michael Murphy destroyer on 27 September, citing a “loss of confidence”, according to a defence official.
The vessel had been deployed to support operations against Iran.
Admiral Brian Monahan, who served as attending physician to Congress and the Supreme Court for nearly 18 years, is also reported to have left his post amid an investigation.
Democratic Representatives Joe Courtney and Adam Smith said the Navy had failed to notify the House Armed Services Committee.
In a letter to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and the service’s top uniformed officer, Admiral Daryl Caudle, they expressed “deep frustration” over the lack of communication.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Saudi Arabia executes former child protester Jawad Qureiris
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/14/2026 - 16:32
Rights groups condemn secret execution of former child protester as a tool of political oppression under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
This picture shows a poster depicting King Salman bin Abdulaziz (R), and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (L) in Riyadh on May 12, 2025 (AFP)
Off
Saudi Arabia executed a man who was detained as a child, alongside another Saudi national from the Kingdom’s Shia-majority Eastern Province.
In a statement on Saturday, the Saudi Press Agency confirmed that Riyadh had executed Jawad Qureiris.
Hailing from a prominent Shia-majority family in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province, Qureiris was a former child defendant who was just 14 to 15 years old during the 2011-12 Arab Spring protests.
Qureiris’ family has a documented history of encounters with state security: one of his brothers was killed by security forces, while another was arrested at age 13 and faced capital charges related to alleged offences committed when he was nine years old.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Interior also announced that Fadel bin Hassan bin Abdullah Al-Safwani was executed on Saturday.
The ministry claimed the men were convicted of “terrorist crimes,” alleging they joined a foreign terrorist organisation, opened fire on security personnel and vehicles with weapons and explosives, possessed live ammunition, and provided logistical and financial support for operations within the Kingdom.
According to the SPA statement, the cases passed through specialised criminal courts, where the men’s legal responsibility was established before the verdicts were upheld by the Supreme Court and ratified via a royal decree.
Qureiris was arrested in December 2020 and charged with offences related to taking part in protests and organising on social media.
